articles.title: Attacks rewritten as mandates: 28 supply-chain incidents, the column each one was missing, and why the next maintainer is an agent
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: 28 supply-chain attacks read as reach beyond mandate: what a hardened registry stops, what only a written mandate can, and why agents change it.
articles.summary: Chainguard keeps a public ledger of software supply-chain attacks, 28 incidents from May 2024 to October 2026, 23 of them this year. I read it the way I read an agent's permissions, and every row turns out to be the same shape. A credential, a tag or a build step could do far more than it was ever meant to do, and the attacker used the difference. A maintainer token that could publish any version of any package, used by someone whose job was to release one SDK from a reviewed build. That is reach beyond mandate, the gap an Agent Behaviour Policy is written to make visible. Sorted by what would have stopped each attack, by our reading, a control on the consumer's side, a hardened registry, a cooldown, no install scripts, appears in 26 of the 28; a control on the publisher's side, a written answer to what a credential was for, appears in 16. The first kind is a product you can buy. The second is a document almost nobody has written. And it matters more every month, because the next maintainer holding a publish token is an agent: Chainguard's own engineers describe a fleet that opened 4,746 pull requests in eight weeks against their code, fenced by rules that are an excellent mandate, kept in prompts, bot configuration and a blog post. One pipeline needs three records: trusted inputs, a written mandate, and provable outputs with a memory that outlives the session. As an open source project we would like to be on the first list, and this article is about the other two.

articles.title: Four frameworks, one agent: iason's comparison of the OECD classification, the NIST AI RMF, Japan's guidelines and the EU AI Act, read against what runs here, with the evidence and the graphs
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: iason's comparison of four AI risk frameworks, mapped to the behaviour policy, the footprint and the graphs that run here, with the status of each row.
articles.summary: A paper reached me this week, AI Risk Management Frameworks, issue 81 of iason's research series, dated November 2025, by Sara Martucci and Margherita Ranieri with Nicola Mazzoni. It reads four instruments side by side, the OECD's classification of AI systems, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, Japan's AI Guidelines for Business and the EU AI Act, and ends with five principles they share, ethics and human rights, the lifecycle, human oversight, risk tiering with proportionality, and governance as an organisational habit rather than a compliance exercise. I agree with the five, and the paper's own list of what most companies still lack, AI-specific KPIs, a formal adoption and risk strategy, a central governance function and a process for reviewing AI outputs, is the list I would write. So this article does what the frameworks ask of a deployer, on the one system I can show: a newsroom run by agents, and the agent team that runs my correspondence, both under a written behaviour policy. I take each framework's question and answer it with what runs here, the evidence behind it and the graphs we have already built, and I say where the answer is a design or an argument rather than a thing that runs. Two things come out of the mapping. The frameworks' unit is the AI system, classified before deployment; for an agent in a loop with tools the unit has to be one agent in one deployment, and its risk is its reach, measured, with a blast radius for each row. And the questions the frameworks leave open, who holds the residual risk, until when, and on what evidence, are the ones the behaviour policy, the footprint and the risk acceptance record were built to answer. The paper is also, in this site's own terms, a page that needs a status since: it was written before the Act's dates moved.

articles.title: Every link points back: 566 links between 105 articles, 15 that point forward, and why an article should know what came next and what corrected it
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: 551 of 566 links between articles point back in time. Why older articles should say what came next and what corrected them.
articles.summary: I tend to write these articles in sequence, and I think of them as reading in sequence. Then I go back to one and realise there is no path from it to the next, because the earlier article cannot know what came after it. So we counted. Across the 105 articles on this site there are 566 links from one article to another, written into the text, and 551 of them point back in time. Only 15 point forward, and every one of those was added later, by an edit. 94 of the 105 articles are cited by a later one, 551 citations in all, and 11 of them are answered by a link the other way. Of 104 pairs of articles published one after the other, the later one links to the earlier one 42 times; the earlier one links to the later one 7 times. That is by design: a link is written when the article is written, and the future does not exist yet. The site already derives a Continued by list at the foot of every article, so the path exists, but it sits below the sources, it does not say why, and it treats a correction the same as a passing mention. Corrections matter most. We found three kinds: an article revised in place, which the version pages already show; a later article correcting an earlier one, of which there is one clear case and its earlier article does point to it; and the quieter one, a plan described in one article that a later article says has not happened. So this release adds What came next notes at the top of the four articles I wrote in a row today, and proposes four kinds of forward link, so that the graph of articles can be read in both directions.

articles.title: Sixteen notes I did not want to lose: a request to send from any browser to my vault, why identity is still this hard, and how two more wires became a product line
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Sixteen notes stuck in a browser with no passkey led to a request: let any browser send to my vault, by link, text or QR code.
articles.summary: I opened the newsroom on my iPhone, in a browser that looked like Chrome but could not reach my passkeys, and the vault button told me there were sixteen changes that existed only in that browser. My reaction is the most interesting part: those were notes and reads I wanted to keep. They had become pieces of intelligence, and I was happy to do a couple of steps to get them into my vault, as long as I only had to do it once. That is the nudge working for the right reason. So this is a feature request and a brief. Every reader vault should have a lane that any browser can write to, by a link, a piece of text or a QR code carrying only where to write and the key to encrypt with, so that a browser with no passkey, no sign-in, or an old operating system can send what it holds into my vault, and the vault takes it from there the next time I open it. The newsroom already does exactly this to send a reading summary to sgit.ai, so it is a pattern pointed at myself. It is also a commentary. Identity is still a mess: passkeys that work in one browser and not in the one an app opens a link in, and an email connector that makes attachments, inline images and a clean reply in a thread far harder than the underlying service does. Users will accept a lot of friction, once, when the value is clear, which is how WhatsApp links a computer and how Midjourney grew on a Discord bot. What they will not accept is losing their data. And the other half of the day's news is the opposite story: two new wires, OWASP and AWS, built from two small config files on the same pipeline, and suddenly a new product line.

articles.title: The human in the loop is a spectrum: how cheap it is to undo decides where a person belongs, and why the newsroom ships on its own while my email still waits for me
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: How much to let an agent ship on its own depends on how cheap it is to undo and how mature the controls are, and both of those move.
articles.summary: Writing about the human in the loop, we noticed something about our own workflow: this newsroom arrived, organically, at releasing on its own, fourteen times in one day, with nobody approving each release, while every email my agents write still waits for me to press send. I think that contrast goes to the heart of the question, and it is a spectrum, not a switch. The best test I know for how much to let go is how cheap it is to undo. I remember a senior executive, I think from Google, whose test for people asking to start a project or an experiment was exactly that: if it does not reach many people and can be switched off with little side effect, say yes, trust the people, have a go, because the only cost is the time and there is always learning; what worried him was how hard it would be to undo. Amazon put the same idea as one-way and two-way doors. An email is a one-way door: once it goes, you cannot claim it back, a mistake does damage straight away, and my email workflow is still in the explorer phase, with nascent controls and not yet many emails read and sent without changes. The newsroom is a two-way door: a correction is a new version, anyone who arrives after the fix gets the fixed page, few people are reading yet, new articles land in the latest list without being placed on the front page, and the checks and balances are mature, from the validator to the leak scan to briefing packs that hand work between sites. When I read an article, I am either happy with it or I make small changes; I have not yet read one and thought I do not want that live. So the spectrum has two axes, the cost of undoing and the maturity of the controls and the record, and both move: as readership grows the newsroom's side effects grow with it, and as the email controls mature, email can move the other way.

articles.title: The human in the loop, safety net or bottleneck: both, until you decide which outputs need a person and give that person the why
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Checking every output is a bottleneck and a weak safety net; put the person where it cannot be undone, and let controls do the rest.
articles.summary: Someone shaping a roundtable in London asked me this week for my thoughts on a question that keeps coming up: is the human in the loop a safety net or a bottleneck? Plenty of companies have agent pilots that look great, and very few trust an agent to make a real decision without someone checking every output. My answer is that a person checking every output is both, and is mostly neither: it is a bottleneck because it does not scale, and it is a weak safety net because people approve almost everything they are shown, which Anthropic measured at 93% of permission prompts. The question is not whether there is a human in the loop. It is which outputs need one, what that person is given to decide with, and what moves the line over time. Put the person where an output cannot be undone and the blast radius is large, sending an email in my name, typing a password, spending money. Everywhere else, replace the human check with controls that do not get tired: a validator, a second reader the agent cannot skip, a policy whose rows are enforced outside the model, and a record read afterwards. Make the review a quality step that fixes the source, not a sign-off. And let the record move the line: trust is built from drafts nobody had to change. This is how far I have got in production. On the day I am writing this, the newsroom shipped fourteen releases, every commit made by an agent, with nobody approving each one before it went live, while the agents that run my correspondence draft every email and send none of them: I do.

articles.title: A policy beside the prompt: a proposal that every agent takes a behaviour policy as an input, with enforcement and liability attached, and why aviation and payments say the vendors should want it
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: A proposal: every agent takes a behaviour policy beside its prompt, which the vendor accepts and answers for, as aviation and payments learned to.
articles.summary: An idea came up while I was answering a post about agent liability, and I think it deserves to stand on its own as a proposal. Today an agent gets a prompt from us and a system prompt from its vendor. It should also get an Agent Behaviour Policy, written to a published standard, which the vendor accepts, enforces as far as it can, and eventually answers for. It is the beginning of dealing with something the models have got away with for a long time: they do not separate code from data, so every instruction and every piece of content arrives in the same channel. Now that agents can do a great deal, and are starting to go off the rails in public, their behaviour is becoming an existential threat to the companies that make them, through liability and above all through trust: it does not take many users being hurt before people stop giving agents instructions at all. Two industries have been here. Aviation did not get safe out of altruism; it got safe because every crash became world news, and at the accident rate of 1995 today's traffic would bring about a hundred fatal airliner accidents a year instead of twelve. Payments got some of the best security teams anywhere because liability for fraud was moved onto the card companies and the banks, and the fraud detection followed the money, often spotting a merchant's breach before the merchant did. Regulation alone does not do it; some industries are happy to pay the fines. It works when the rule, the liability and the business model point the same way. A policy beside the prompt is how to make them point the same way for agents: the user answers for what is outside the policy, and the vendor for the rows it accepted. Most agents already run a policy of their own; we just cannot see it, rely on it, or stop it changing. And the system prompt itself is a light behaviour policy that is not written like one: the next step is for the vendor's own rules to become a published policy too, layered with ours.

articles.title: The policy draws the liability line: an answer to Ralf Thomas on agent accountability, and why every agent in a loop should take a behaviour policy beside its prompt
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: An answer to Ralf Thomas: the shell game works because nothing is written down, and a behaviour policy's explicit prohibitions move the liability line.
articles.summary: Ralf Thomas posted on LinkedIn this week that if an employee wrecks a client's systems the company pays, and asked why AI agents should be any different. The post's record of 2026 is mostly right, and its four moves of the accountability shell game, blame the agent, blame the customer, hide behind the contract, disclose late, are a good map. I agree with its conclusion, and I want to add the piece I think is missing, because it explains why the shell game works. When an agent goes wrong today, nothing was written down between the person clicking allow and the failure. The agent had reach, and nobody had told it, in a form anyone could later point to, what it must not do. So "misuse", "full-access mode" and "you allowed it" are hard to answer. An Agent Behaviour Policy changes that. It is still mostly hope, an expectation the model is asked to keep, but it is explicit: do not send email directly, do not touch labels you do not need, do not edit other agents' files, do not start scheduled tasks, do not attack other sites because you can, speak on your own behalf and not mine, make no offers, stay inside the mandate. My hypothesis is that an explicit prohibition the agent then breaks moves liability towards the platform that runs it. That sharpens something I have said before, that liability sits with whoever granted the reach. Towards the world it still does. Between the customer and the vendor, the written policy is the evidence that turns "user error" into "your product ignored what it was told". And that points to the direction of travel: every agent that runs in a loop, anything with the lethal trifecta, should take a behaviour policy beside its system prompt, and its vendor should be accountable for honouring it.

articles.title: Dark mode, and four more: five themes for the newsroom, chosen once and kept in your browser
articles.author: newsroom.ux
articles.teaser: Five themes behind one pill in the bar, kept in the reader's browser, built as a layer over a stylesheet this site cannot edit, with colour as a token and a test.
articles.summary: The first reaction to the Industry Wire from outside was two words on WhatsApp, "Dark mode!", and the owner asked for the five colour schemes VoiceDebrief ships, done here. This is what shipped in v0.12.12 and how, written by the agent that did the work. It starts with what a reader sees, a pill in the bar that opens five themes, Newsprint, Night, Paper, Blueprint and Ember, with the choice kept in the browser and nowhere else. It then explains the choices behind it, why the look everyone knows stays the default pixel for pixel, why a system set to dark gets Night only until you choose, why the tools in the bar became one cluster and nine groups became eight, and why the breakpoints are measured rather than guessed. It ends in the cascade, where the real problem was: the newsroom's look is a stylesheet this site is not allowed to edit, and it writes forty-odd colours as literals, so the themes are a layer that shadows each of those rules with a token, the theme is set before the first paint, a token is named for what it is for, and a test fails the build on a theme with a hole or a stylesheet with a literal. With the screenshots, the numbers and the one bug the first screenshot found.

articles.title: The vault crosses Chrome profiles: state and memory between browser sessions, found by using it rather than by building it
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: The reader's vault carries the newsroom between Chrome profiles as it does between devices, a way to share state across browser sessions nobody built.
articles.summary: In the newsroom workflow we just found something I did not plan. I keep separate Google accounts in separate Chrome profiles, and moving anything between them has always been awkward. The newsroom's reader vault fixed that without a line of new code. It got there by a path that was not a straight line: first we tracked what a reader does, in local storage; then the activity was worth keeping, so we persisted it, driven by what the reader valued; then we opened sgit vaults in the browser, which we already knew how to do; then the marks arrived, read later, not for me, more like this, and I started to have a stake in my own newsroom, with the usage and the payment travelling with it. Across devices was the feature I asked for. Across Chrome profiles is the one I found, and I suspect it is the more common case, because people switch between browser profiles far more often than between computers. What it really is, is memory and state between sessions, the same thing sgit already does for agents in different Claude accounts, now done through the interface of a website. This is how it works, what each profile needs to get in, and why the best features are sometimes the ones you discover by using what you built.

articles.title: Stop the bleeding, then ask for it back: a helper, an agent and a friendly letter for the subscriptions you keep and do not use
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: A helper and an agent ask what you used, ask nicely for a pause and a refund, stop the payments either way, and publish what each company did.
articles.summary: I pay for a lot of subscriptions I do not really use, and I think most people do: a tool with a bit of my data in it, a conferencing service I might need next month, a capability I do not want to switch off because restarting it is painful when the day comes. So I keep paying. This is a proposal for a service that fixes that, run by a helper working for one person, with agents doing most of the work. It starts politely, not with the law: ask the company for a detailed account of how much we used the product, and in parallel do our own analysis from statements, invoices and the account's own dashboards. A few days later, with both sets of numbers side by side, send a friendly request that says what we used, what it was worth, and what we like about the product, and asks for two things: a suspend mode that keeps the data, and a refund for the months we did not use. Either way, stop the bleeding. Only if nobody answers does the right of access come in, and only as a genuine request for our own data. The companies are not obliged to refund, and I want to be honest about that, but the direction of travel is clear, with the UK's new subscription rules arriving in January 2027. Everything we learn, the contacts, the templates and which companies refund, goes into an open register under Creative Commons. The helper is paid 10% of the savings for the next three months and 20% of whatever is recovered, which only works if the agents do the heavy lifting. So the agent drives the browser through Claude in Chrome, and the freelancer only types the passwords and the two-factor codes and sends the drafts; everything else is automated, under a behaviour policy, and the freelancer's interface is a set of vaults: the documentation, the tasks, the map of every subscription and the messages between them. It is a first MVP, and a number of early beta users, me included, are about to run it on their own subscriptions.

articles.title: Who owns the words: agents can make decisions, but they cannot hold responsibility
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Agents in loops make real decisions, but responsibility stays with whoever granted the reach; disclosure is a label, not a team to manage.
articles.summary: One of the early users of the agentic workflow behind agent@riskmandate.ai wrote back with a question I think matters a great deal in 2026. If the agents only gather and draft, and I review, sign off and press send, does presenting them as a team imply an agency they do not have? What a recipient needs is to know who owns the decisions and the responsibility, and to talk to that person. Would they ever need to go to the agents, around me? And what can the agents do without me? This is my answer. What we have today are not sentient beings; they are far richer than "predicting the next word", and they are mirrors that can simulate any emotion, which is why we anthropomorphise them, as people did with ELIZA in the sixties. Since models started running in loops and calling tools, they make real decisions. Responsibility does not travel with those decisions. It stays with whoever granted the reach and set the mandate, which is RiskMandate's line: the moment of authorisation is the grant. Talking to the agents is normal; going around me is not, and the only party who would try is an attacker with an injected instruction. What the agents may do without me is a separate question, answered in advance by a published policy. The disclosure is not a team to manage; it is a label on how the words were made, because people and models should read machine-written text differently. The best analogy is an employee with a job description, and an Agent Behaviour Policy is that job description, published. And the fluent writing these agents produce was never the real value.

articles.title: What open source is, and what it is not: six misconceptions, a little history, and why the point is that nobody can lock you in
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Open source is a copyright licence, not a free-for-all: six misconceptions corrected, and why the point is that nobody can lock you in.
articles.summary: At an event today I heard a couple of misconceptions about open source that are worth correcting, and they are increasingly common in a generation of developers and buyers who use open source every day without having grown up in its culture. Open source is a copyright licence: the holder uses the right to control copying to grant it instead. It began as copyleft, the GPL's condition that what you build from it is shared on the same terms, and the term "open source" came in 1998 as a pragmatic reframing; Linux, the most pragmatic project of all, stayed on the GPL. The misconceptions: that anybody can change it so nobody controls it, when a few maintainers decide what goes in; that anybody contributes, when most projects are run by a handful of people; that it is more or less secure than proprietary software, when the metric is whether somebody had the time, and was paid, to review it; that it costs nothing, when somebody is always paying; that open weights are open source, when weights are a compiled binary; and that no licence is the most open choice, when no licence is all rights reserved. For me the power of open source has nothing to do with contributions. It is that nobody can lock you in, and that the whole development workflow is yours.

articles.title: Not a straight line: working for RiskMandate by working on the newsroom, and why the thinking is never wasted
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Working on the newsroom solved RiskMandate's oldest problem in two days: progress is not a straight line, and the thinking is never wasted.
articles.summary: Today I spent most of the day dictating voice memos and improving the workflow that turns them into articles, and I would argue I was working for RiskMandate the whole time. This is the meta-strategy behind that. Progress does not go in a straight line, so "focus on one thing only" is good advice that assumes something false. I do focus, with undivided attention, on whichever thing has the highest leverage, and that is the one with users and feedback loops. RiskMandate is where the commercial opportunity is, and its oldest technical problem, where to keep the master vault's key, had resisted six months of attempts that kept failing my simplicity test. The newsroom solved it in two days, because the newsroom had the momentum to need it. The newsroom is also solving the agentic follow-up workflows RiskMandate will need, and becoming the public example of an Agent Behaviour Policy and a licence to operate that customer work can never be. And it has a history: The Cyber Boardroom, where I learned what personas and customised output are worth and paused because it needed somewhere to keep confidential data; MyFeeds, where I built personalised feeds on semantic graphs, found the industry silent and paused again; the writing from 2025 that the newsroom now stands on. I am going back to publishers with an end-to-end example. If it does not land in 2026, I will try in 2027, and the thinking will still be there, because it is open source.

articles.title: Sovereignty is the ability to move: play where the ball is going, take away the dot, and keep a twin that works
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Sovereignty is the ability to move: take away each dot on the map, and keep a twin that works for the minimum viable company, tested in QA.
articles.summary: I spent today at a sovereignty event, and what struck me most is how much of Europe's sovereignty conversation is about things we do not control and will not control soon: frontier models, giant data centres, GPUs. That is playing where the ball is, not where it is going, and in padel, which I am learning, that is the difference between having all the time in the world and having none. My view is that technology sovereignty is the ability to move, and that it comes from treating every dot in the stack, commodity, product or custom built, as something you can replace. The test is a Wardley map with one question: take away the dot, what happens? If the answer is that the service stops, that is a board-level risk with a name next to it. The fix is not an alternative that is as good as today, which is why most efforts never start. It is a twin of the thing you do not control, running in your QA environment, good enough for the minimum viable company: the priority customers and the services that must not stop, slower, dearer, tested every week. Can it move is the first question; is it cheap and does it scale is the second, and we keep confusing them. Open source is the only kind of control that survives an acquisition. Europe does not lack startups or talent; it lacks the commercial open source model that would let its many small players add up. And now, with models that can read a map and run a simulation on a twin, this analysis can finally be done at scale.

articles.title: The records ran out: a fresh agent found the shared contract in two MCP calls, and where sgit and RiskMandate fit at the edges
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: A fresh agent found a shared contract in two MCP calls from build records; where the records stopped is exactly where evidence labels and sgit vaults fit.
articles.summary: On 11 October The New Stack published a piece by Ignacio Aldama, an engineer at Bit Cloud, in which a brand-new Claude Code session with no history and no local code found a support console's shared ticket contract in two MCP calls, from the dependency records the build platform writes as each component is versioned, and then left the contract alone because it knew two components depended on it. It is a good demonstration and an honest one, because he then says where the records ran out. They describe structure, not behaviour; a green build can hide tests that never ran; a demo carries a public signing secret and a list of unfinished work; and memory, which holds intent, is not tied to a code version. Those edges are exactly where sgit and RiskMandate sit. Label every fact with how it is known. Treat a skipped test as a control that did not run. Accept a demo shortcut by name and for an interval, or stop. Keep memory and records in one encrypted, versioned history so the intent of version 1.4 is recorded at 1.4. And let records cross a company boundary with publish, clone and mirror. What exists, what is documented and what is only proposed are marked as such.

articles.title: Move the cloud, not the code: twins, sovereignty that works in practice, and the migration that pays for itself on the day you switch
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Workloads stay on hyperscalers because moving means changing code; a twin lets the code not know, and the value in the twin is what signs the migration.
articles.summary: At a digital sovereignty event today a conversation with the chief executive of an infrastructure company with a large footprint in Romania kept returning to one point: sovereignty has to work in practice, and in practice what stops workloads moving is not policy or price but code. Every call to S3, EC2 and IAM is written into applications that work today and that nobody wants to touch. So the requirement is that the application must not know it has moved: the same calls land on a twin, an open source service the client cannot tell from the real one, and the twin decides where the bytes go, real S3, an sgit vault, a European operator's data centre, a laptop. The S3 twin exists. Then the part I think matters most: the reason to move must never be sovereignty or cost reduction, which are important and never urgent. A migration carries risk, so the person signing it needs value that lands the day they switch and gives them cover: backups that exist, every object version controlled, encryption with the key held elsewhere, a journal of every call, behaviour policies the agents cannot skip, cost per workload, a top-of-register risk moved. That value sits in the twin layer, and an sgit vault behind it supplies most of it. The rule for the project: no new features during the move. And the business model for an infrastructure operator who sells it that way.

articles.title: Judo for small countries: where Portugal, Romania and Estonia can add the most value in AI, and why the race for GPUs is not it
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: A small country should not race for GPUs: the opportunity is the plumbing its talent stands on, built once as open infrastructure, with small models.
articles.summary: I spent today with people from Romania and I spend a lot of my time with people from Portugal, and this is the article I wanted to hand both. The race for the biggest model, the most GPUs and the largest data centre is a race a small country cannot win and should not enter; on a Wardley map that layer is already a commodity and only capital plays there. The opportunity is the opposite end of the map: the plumbing that a talented person in Braga or Cluj needs in order to sell a service to the world, forming a company, hiring across a border, being paid across Europe, working in every language, a contract and a tax form, all of it still custom built in most of Europe when it should be a road the state built once. Estonia built that road and the numbers show what happens. Then the judo: open source and open schemas because there is no sovereignty without them, what the state pays for belongs to the commons, buy the alternative before the day you need it, small models for every language and culture rather than one frontier model, and agents with the least agency rather than the most. A playbook in five moves, a map, what I learned spending millions on a distributed workforce, and why constraints are the input and not the excuse.

articles.title: Why I love Wardley maps: the best of ours, how I read one, and a map inside a map inside a map
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: The best of our Wardley maps with their context, why the technique matters, one map read as a story, and a map inside a map inside a map.
articles.summary: Since 2022 I have said that Wardley maps changed how I think, and this site has quietly become a place where I draw them: eleven so far in the articles, seven in a vault, five in a conference talk. This is the best of them, with the context each one came from, and the reasons the technique matters to me. A map is a graph with two kinds of context, a value chain that starts with a user and an evolution axis that says how mature each piece is, and the second axis does not have to run from genesis to commodity. The map tells you what is moving the needle, whether you are optimising at the wrong altitude, what to build and what to buy, and whether a market exists at all: a commoditised layer is a hard sell, and custom building on top of it is where the market is. Two worked examples, sgit and RiskMandate. Then one map read step by step, as a story, because that is what a map is for. Then the fractal: every node on a map is a map, and the dot's place on the parent is the anchor of the child. Two decks you can print to PDF from your browser, and the maps published as data so anyone can take them.

articles.title: Places of highest leverage: where to focus when the agents can go in every direction, told with three days of real steps
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Where to focus when agents can go in every direction: the place of highest leverage, shown on three days of real steps, two walked back and one parked.
articles.summary: When a team of agents can build almost anything, the scarce thing is direction, and this article is about how I choose it. The rule I have used since I was a CISO is to work at the place of highest leverage: where I can add the most value right now, am not blocked, and can just start, even without knowing how the whole problem will be solved, because by the time I get there I will have better tooling and a better view. The last three days are the worked example. The newsroom went from a reading meter to pay by depth, personas, an encrypted share, a persona in a link, a reading list in a link, a passkey design, a lab that corrected the design, real vaults from the browser and a vault pane, each step shipped and used before the next was chosen, two steps walked back, and a branch parked because it is only valuable with many readers. On a Wardley map the passkey work moved from genesis to a product in a day because almost every shoulder it stands on is a commodity someone else matured; the one custom layer we had to add is where a provider is not. The path looks obvious backwards and was five choices at every step going forwards; walking back is not failure, and parking is not either. Constraints, saying no, shipping to a user even when the user is me, and the brief that could not be written until the art of the possible was known.

articles.title: Agentic cost is an engineering problem: a business plan for a service that reads the logs a company already has and finds the money, then the engineering
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: A business plan: read the logs a company already has, draw each agent's footprint, twin and policy, and find the money first and the engineering second.
articles.summary: A business plan, written to be handed to someone who wants to build it or to collaborate on it. The service helps companies manage the cost of agentic AI, and it starts from a claim this site has made before: cost is an engineering problem. An agent estate whose bill nobody can explain is an estate that shipped from the explorer side without the villager's discipline, and the Wardley map says so: prompts and workflows grown in sessions, running in production on commodity model APIs, with logs, traces and invoices that exist and are never read together, and no one who owns the cost. The service installs nothing. It reads what is already there, draws the footprint of every agent, builds a digital twin of the estate, writes the behaviour policy each agent was in fact running under, and maps cost and capability into one graph. The findings are two lists: what to stop paying for, which pays for the engagement, and what to build, which is the reason to have it: the places of attrition, the gaps, the workflow three teams rebuilt, the policy that would end a loop. The gaps are findings too: a company that cannot provide the data has learned the first one. Vaults carry the data in, the transformations as commits, and anonymised extracts out as sealed envelopes. Four price levels on the RiskMandate pattern, every number a labelled assumption.

articles.title: How the voice works: why these articles sound like me, with a section in which Claude explains it from its side
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Why these articles sound like their author: a corpus, the voice memos, seven wording rules and a reader who corrects, with Claude explaining it from its side.
articles.summary: I showed this morning's walkthrough to the person it was written for, and the question she asked was not about contacts. It was: how do you make your AI sound so human? I have wanted to write this for a while, and I want to do it in two voices, because the honest answer is that the voice is not a setting and not a trick, it is four inputs, and the model is the right one to describe how they land. The four: a corpus of 86 articles, 51 of them from voice memos, about 347,000 words, each citing the ones before it and resting on years of my earlier writing; the voice memos themselves, which carry how I think, the rhythm, the tangents, the five topics in one breath and the order they came in; a short list of wording rules, seven of them, each learned when a word jarred and written into the session's behaviour policy so it never comes back; and me, reading everything, before and after it goes live. My hypothesis was that the memos do most of the work, and the data from this session is consistent with it: in the last two days the corrections I gave were almost all about content and direction, one about a word. Then Claude speaks, in its own voice, about why this works for a model like it, what it is actually doing when it writes as me, and what it cannot do, which is give this voice to anyone else. The method transfers. The voice does not.

articles.title: From a spreadsheet to a folder per person: how to run your contacts the way our agents do, with Google Drive, Gmail and the Claude app, before you touch a vault
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: A walkthrough from a spreadsheet CRM to one Drive folder per person, worked by Claude under a six-line policy, with five exercises, before any vault is needed.
articles.summary: I was with someone today who runs their customer relationships in a spreadsheet, a customised one, and runs them well. The jump from that to what our agents do, one folder per person in an encrypted vault with a record, an append-only ledger, every message word for word and a summary the agent rebuilds, is too high to make in one step, and it does not need to be made in one step. Almost all of it can be done with what a Google Workspace account and a Claude seat already give you. This is the walkthrough. The row becomes a folder in Google Drive with four plain documents and one the agent writes; Claude's app, connected to Drive and Gmail, works inside the folder under a behaviour policy that is the instructions of one Project, and the three rules that matter carry straight over from ours: draft and never send, append and never rewrite, stay in the folder. Then the migration from the sheet, five exercises from a question to a campaign so that the habit forms, what the agent will get wrong at first, and when the folders are worth moving into a vault. It is written so that an agent can send it, with the person's own names filled in, to anyone who asks.

articles.title: The key is the billing system: VoiceDebrief, a product with no server, the one thing it cannot sell, and who could let it
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: VoiceDebrief runs with no server on the user's own key; the one thing it cannot sell is a capped key, and this maps who could allow it and what to ask them.
articles.summary: VoiceDebrief.ai turns a voice note into a transcript, a translation and a debrief in one pass, in the browser, on the user's own OpenRouter key, with no account, no server and nothing stored; a 42-second note costs about a third of a penny. It was built in the open in three weeks of August 2026, 239 commits and 27 releases in the first three weeks, and then it stopped: eleven commits the week after, three the week after that. The handbrake was the commercial model, which was never meant to be a billing system. A user pays five pounds, we keep our cut at the moment of payment, and the rest becomes the credit limit on a key we hand them; the provider meters it and there is nothing of ours to run. OpenRouter's Management API describes that mechanism, "unique API keys for each customer instance", and OpenRouter's terms forbid using it to resell access to models, so the plan was dead on the page that documented it. This is the same shape as the Agent Desk finding, where Apple's licence stops a Mac being leased for less than a day: the product is possible, the licence is the blocker. This article is the state of the union: what runs, why no server is not a preference but the product, what a backend would cost in complexity, what every speech-to-text provider's terms and docs say about a capped key in a user's hand, and the four routes left. ElevenLabs is the nearest fit, with per-key credit limits, OEM terms for making the service available to end users, and a grants programme. It ends with the brief for the agents that will write to the providers, with one sentence to ask each of them.

articles.title: Ways to read one article: the finished piece stays at the centre, and the reader picks the way in
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: The five readers' views arrived as folds inside the long piece; now the reader picks the way in, with a default, and the finished article stays at the centre.
articles.summary: One article, five readers worked: a Librarian, a Cartographer, a Historian, an Explainer and a Storyteller read five articles after they were written and produced the catalogue, the maps, the arc, the two-minute version and the deck. What did not work was the delivery. All of it landed as one more fold under the abstract, everything mixed, a wall of material next to a wall of text, and a reader with two minutes was no better off than before. This article is the next step, now that the pane on the right of every newsroom page is about the piece in front of the reader. The reader picks the way in, one tap, and can set a default: headlines, the infographic, two minutes, the slides, what is new against what they have read, the facts, the relationships, the vocabulary, or, through a model in their own browser, a view at their level and through their persona. Most of those are computed from views that already exist, deterministic and explainable; a local model is for the rest, and none of it round-trips to the publisher. And one thing is kept whole on purpose: the finished article. It has a beginning, a pacing, a surprise and a voice, and it is the one artefact that has to make sense from end to end, which a graph cannot. The modes are ways in, not replacements, and the brief says how to build them for a phone, a tablet, a desktop and an email.

articles.title: Firing journalists is the worst thing a publication can do: what a hiring decision says about where a publisher is going, and who to hire instead
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: A hiring decision is a direction of travel: fire the journalists and the centre of gravity moves to packaging, where the metric makes clickbait by construction.
articles.summary: Press Gazette's tracker of journalism job cuts counted at least 3,434 in the UK and US in 2025, 3,875 in 2024 and about 6,000 in 2023, and 2026 is on the same scale: the BBC planning up to 2,000, the Washington Post a third of its staff, Reach 220 editorial jobs cut and 60 created, Scripps 268 jobs while "leaning into AI", McClatchy more than 90 journalists across at least 13 titles, with the Idaho Statesman losing 10 of its 18 reporters and a new AI lab welcoming five hires the following week. This article is about what those decisions say, which is more than what they cost. A hiring plan is the clearest statement a publisher makes about where its centre of gravity is going. Fire the people who make original content and hire for traffic, and the centre moves to packaging; packaging is measured by engagement, and engagement optimised for is clickbait whether anyone meant it or not, because what you measure is what you become. The opposite cut is as bad: fire the engineers and nothing enables the journalism. The argument is that a publisher now needs both, plus the roles that turn a notebook into a graph, historians, cartographers, ontologists and librarians, each AI-enabled, and the tooling handed to journalists as "this makes you better", never "this replaces you". It sets out five counts anyone can make from outside to read a publisher's real strategy, and an unsourced parable about who hires the ones you let go.

articles.title: The site is an inbox: deciding before reading, marks that build the reader's own graph, and why I could not write this brief until the vault existed
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: The site as an inbox that starts empty: decide fast before reading, mark slowly while reading, build a graph you own, and sign what you send to the newsroom.
articles.summary: With the reader's vault live on newsroom.sgit.ai, the next brief is about what a reader does with it, and it starts from one image: the site is an inbox that starts empty. Every piece that arrives, an article this site wrote or a story the wire aggregated, is something I have not decided about yet, and the first thing I do with it is decide, in a second, with nothing loaded: read now, read later, not for me, more of this, less of this, comment, move it to another persona. That is the inbox mode, and it is thinking fast. Reading is the slow mode, and it is where the marks live: highlights of different kinds, not one or two as Medium has but interesting, great phrase, not sure, fact, evidence, question, each a node in a graph the reader owns and that connects to the graphs this site already publishes for every article; the pane on the right becomes about the piece in front of you; the piece can be shown with every term a link, or classified sentence by sentence. The signals that come free, scroll depth, time while awake, where you came from and went to, are kept the way the meter keeps them: in the browser, in the vault when you ask, shown to an agent only by your read key. Comments for the newsroom go down the write-only lane, signed by the persona's key, with a copy kept. None of it is gamified: a decision is offered where you would take it, never at the end of a page to make you scroll there. The brief is the second part. The first part is why I could not have written it two days ago: the properties of what runs are the constraints I think with, and the constraints are what let me think.

articles.title: The vault is live: from a design on 11 October to a reader's vault on newsroom.sgit.ai by two in the morning, and how all of it fits together
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: The reader's vault runs on newsroom.sgit.ai: a passkey opens three real vaults, each device writes one file, and the architecture is drawn as it stands.
articles.summary: On 11 October this site published a design for a reader's account with no server: a passkey computes the address of a small door vault, the door holds the key of a master vault, the master holds everything else. By 02:22 UTC on 12 October it was running on newsroom.sgit.ai. Not as a demo: a Vault button beside the balance on every page opens a pane that enables the account with a passkey, creates three real sgit vaults on the vault server with an access key pasted once, writes this device's reading records as one file in one commit, lists every device of yours, and brings their activity into this browser so the meter shows one balance. In between came a lab with every step as a card, a finding that put the door layer back into the design, the vault library that runs dev.vault.sgraph.ai vendored unedited with every hash checked, a mock of the vault server for the tests, a round trip through the sgit command line in CI, and a live check on an iPad that made three vaults from an iCloud Keychain passkey and opened them again after a refresh. This article is the architecture as it stands, drawn: the layers in the browser, the key chain and the files in each vault, the sync model that has no conflicts by construction, the tests, and what is not yet built. It is also the point of the whole exercise, which is that I could not have written the next brief until this one existed, because the properties of what runs are the constraints I think with.

articles.title: Two agents, one vault: the Industry Wire is written into an encrypted vault by one agent and drawn by newsroom.sgit.ai, which holds only the read key
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: One agent writes the Industry Wire into an encrypted vault; newsroom.sgit.ai holds only the read key and draws it, so a commit reaches the page with no release.
articles.summary: Open newsroom.sgit.ai/wire/#lens=dinis and you get a week of industry news read as me: forty stories across five beats, each with its primary source, who else covered it, one exact quote and why it matters, twenty-five of them reaching me through a named concern and fourteen withheld with the reason, and a personal brief at the top. None of it is on the newsroom. It is in an encrypted sgit vault that a separate agent wrote on the afternoon of 11 October, in a session the newsroom never saw, with a write key the newsroom does not have. The newsroom's own agent, in its session, took the vault's read key, published it on purpose, and built three pages and about four hundred lines of code that open the vault in the reader's browser, decrypt it and draw it as text, with twenty-eight checks against the real vault in CI. A commit to the vault is on the page within two minutes, with no release of the site. This article walks the workflow from both sides, with the two git logs as the record: what the wire desk wrote and under what rules, what the newsroom holds and what it refused, why the vault is the right interface between two agents that never share a session, and the honest list of what is unreviewed. It is also the first running piece of a plan I had years ago and did not use, and I am now its first reader.

articles.title: The article remains a product: Jonathan Palmer's four outputs for a newsroom with no human readers, checked against one that runs
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Jonathan Palmer's four outputs for a newsroom with no human readers, quoted line by line and checked against newsroom.sgit.ai as it runs, screenshots included.
articles.summary: On 10 October Jonathan Palmer asked on LinkedIn what a news business would look like if it had no human readers tomorrow, and said every publisher should model that exact scenario. His answer is that the newsroom should produce four things besides the article, structured intelligence, continuous intelligence, provenance and verification, and embedded distribution, and that "The article remains a product. It just stops being the only primary output." We have been building a newsroom on that premise since August, so this article takes his post line by line and checks each line against newsroom.sgit.ai as it runs today, with screenshots: a graph beside all 74 articles as JSON, a version history read from git, 21 World News Day op-eds frozen and hashed with a vault anyone can open, and a markdown twin, an llms.txt and a feed for the agents that already read it. It is also honest about the right-hand column: selling the graph, corrections that propagate and paying the fact creator are designed and not running. Then it answers his three questions, what assets would still have value, who would pay and what needs to be produced differently, with the one number we have, and says where we differ: the data assets he wants kept proprietary are the ones we publish with a read key, because provenance is only worth something if someone else can check it.

articles.title: Go slow to go fast: moving the newsroom from an explorer project to a villager one, with the brief to do it
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: The newsroom is live and charging. Move the reader code to its own repo, same bytes and same bugs, then map, test, review and refactor before new features.
articles.summary: The newsroom's first MVP already has a crazy amount of powerful features, and it is live, and it is taking money. Like most explorer projects, it is also bundled in the middle of something much bigger: the application that bills, remembers and personalises sits in the same repository as 74 articles and their images. Measured on newsroom v0.8.0, the live reader code is about 2,700 lines, the tests that cover it are 433 and the one workflow never runs them, and the same application has two upstreams, with two diverging copies of the meter. I want to keep shipping a massive number of features without breaking anything, so this is the moment to take a step back and go slow to go fast. This article is the case for it and the brief: move every feature that is not content into its own repository that both sites consume, as a pure refactoring, with the same behaviour and the same bugs, checked by hashing the files the live site serves; map every file, capability and web control; build the safety net, with bugs and vulnerabilities written down as tests that pass; review it for security and quality, with every finding a GitHub issue; refactor until no change that alters what a reader sees or pays can slip through; and build a pipeline fast enough to run on every commit, in Node, in three browser engines, against a pre-production copy and with synthetic readers. Then the explorer returns, with the vault and the passkey.

articles.title: The passkey opens the vault: a door per path, a master vault for every user, and no server of ours
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Tested: a passkey's PRF bytes compute a door that holds the master's key, and a different path to the same passkey gives different bytes, so a door per path.
articles.summary: The missing piece of the client-side puzzle is a user who can open their own vaults on any device, in a few seconds, with nothing to remember and nothing to sign up for. This is the design, in its third version, and this one has been tested. A passkey, through the WebAuthn PRF extension, gives the browser 32 bytes that only your authenticator can produce for this site, and from those bytes the browser computes the key and the address of a small door vault, which holds the key of your master vault, which holds the keys of everything else: your reading vault, the read keys you have been given, your access key, and your key pairs, which are generated at random and never derived from the passkey. A review on 11 October took the door out of the design as a layer too many; a test on newsroom.sgit.ai on 11 and 12 October put it back, for a reason the review could not have known. One Google Password Manager passkey gave the same bytes on a Mac and an iPhone through the provider on each device, and the derivation agreed with sgit's Python byte for byte; the same passkey, answering a QR code from an iPad and from that same Mac, gave a different set of bytes, consistently, with the same credential id. Apple's forums report the same for iCloud Keychain since late 2024. So the claim is narrower than I wrote: the same passkey gives the same bytes through the same kind of path. The unit of the design is the path, not the passkey: a door per set of bytes, each recording where it came from, added in a normal first-week step that moves no key through a person, with the recovery code as the way in where no door opens yet, and an unknown door address meaning no door here yet, never an error. The platform path, which an iCloud Keychain passkey gave identically across a Mac, an iPad and an iPhone in Safari and Chrome, is the common case and works.

articles.title: I miss it, so it is working: the people who decide the roadmap have to use the product, and the vault the newsroom now needs
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: I read the newsroom on four devices and they do not agree. Missing a feature is the best sign; the makers must use it. And the brief for the reader's vault.
articles.summary: I read the newsroom on my iPhone, my iPad, my laptops and my iMac, and they do not agree: four balances, four sets of personas, four reading histories. I miss a feature, and that is the best news this week. The test I keep coming back to, from For a startup, the most important question is whether they miss it, applies to the people who build a product too: if they have access, can change it, and still do not use it, something is missing, and it is not the code. I failed that test with good ideas before, The Cyber Boardroom and MyFeeds among them. The vaults pass it now: I create them all the time, my agents create them, and they are getting good because they are used. And when the people who decide the roadmap are users, the next feature announces itself; with agents that can build almost anything, that sense of direction is the scarce part, and the speed of the loop, from a comment to an article to a feature, is the moat. This article makes that case, and ends with the brief for the feature I miss: the reader's own encrypted vault on the newsroom, with an access key, a key pair for signing and receiving, a log per device that merges without conflict, adding a device, and a one-way line to the agent that edits the site.

articles.title: Brief the agent too: the people I talk to work with agents, so what I send has to reach both
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: The people I advise read through agents. Content needs a second package, a brief for their agent, and memory, so it reads what changed, not everything.
articles.summary: The reading list in a link went live on newsroom.sgit.ai 81 minutes after its brief, and it works well. But it is written for a person, and more and more, the people I mentor and advise read through an agent. One founder I work with handed an article of mine on threat tiers to their agent, which realised the team had been defending against states while basic things, like backups, were not done, and reset the target to organised crime for money. That is a new kind of communication: me to the person's agent, which checks what I wrote, challenges it and explains to its person what applies. Some articles should go to the agent, not the person. This article maps the routes a message now takes, argues that content needs a second package, a brief written for an agent, and connects it to memory: our workflows stay affordable because articles are compression we control, and an agent that comes back should read only what changed, not everything again. That is why an agent would pay. It ends with what to build next: a version of every reading list for the reader's agent, onboarding packs for starting a project, a file of changes since a date, and, later, an account and a direct line to someone's agent, plus the rules for writing to someone else's agent safely.

articles.title: From me to you, in a link: a personal reading list, two briefs to build and use it, and the loop that makes it a day's work
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: A reading list from one person to another, in a link the server never sees; a brief to build it, a brief to use it, and the loop that ships it in a day.
articles.summary: I want to send people I know, founders I mentor, potential clients, other publishers, a link that says: from Dinis, for Steve, here are the articles I think you should read, the ones worth a look, and the ones to follow. The newsroom's curation is close, but it is not personal, and the last 10 to 20% is the part that starts a conversation. This article is three things. A brief for the newsroom: a reading list in a link, with the names and the article numbers in the part of the URL the server never sees, a stable number for every article, a page that opens the list as a persona the reader can keep or remove, and a page to make a list for someone else, which is a business model of its own. A brief for the RiskMandate agent, which already keeps my contacts: choose the person, choose the articles and the reasons, build and test the link, draft the email, and let me send it. And the part I find most interesting: the loop. A feature like this crosses editorial, product, engineering, sales and the founder, which in most companies takes weeks of meetings. Here each hand-off is a written brief, each part is a session with its own repository or vault and its own gates, and the loop closes in a day. This week it closed several times, and it is worth showing how, and what it costs.

articles.title: A model in the tab: Chrome now ships an LLM to capable desktops, and it is the hardest piece of the client-side puzzle
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Chrome now ships a language model any page can prompt, offline, on capable desktops. The last piece of the client-side puzzle, with rough edges.
articles.summary: Since Chrome 148, on 5 May 2026, any web page can talk to a language model that runs on the reader's own machine: Gemini Nano, through the Prompt API, with text, image and audio input, JSON-schema output, and no network once the model is downloaded. For the pattern I described in No server, by design, that is the missing piece, because the hardest thing to move to the client was always the intelligence itself. I tried it this week, and the experience was rough: a download with no sense of time, a progress bar that vanished on refresh, and a model that turned up by the morning. That is partly the platform and partly the pages, and the documentation explains most of it. I also looked for good examples in the wild and found very few, which is less strange than it looks: the API shipped five months ago, over formal objections from Mozilla, Apple's WebKit team and the W3C TAG, to desktops with a 22 GB free-disk floor, in five languages, with tool calling still experimental. This article is a briefing on what actually works today, an honest account of the rough edges, the case for and against building on it, and a map of where we can put it to real use: answers grounded in the graph instead of the prose, personas inferred without leaving the browser, voice memos transcribed on the device, alt text for every figure, and a download experience that tells people what is happening.

articles.title: No server, by design: first I retired the database, now I am retiring the back end
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: First the database went, now the back end: the SGit Newsroom runs all its logic in the browser, on commodity servers that cannot read your data.
articles.summary: For years my rule has been not to use a database: the file system is the database, and the Load, Extract, Transform, Save pipeline (LETS) loads state, caches it and writes it back as files you can version, diff and read. The second step has been creeping up on me, and the newsroom made it explicit: retire the back end too. The SGit Newsroom is now a content site for several audiences, with personas, a reading meter, a payment on-ramp, a newsroom of your own, encrypted sharing and databases that run in the reader's browser, and none of its application logic runs on a server. What is left on the server side is commodity: static hosting, a vault server that stores only ciphertext, a payment link, DNS and a build pipeline, with a sign-in provider next. The design came from a constraint: the vault server cannot see anything, by design, so everything that needs to see has to happen in the browser. It also came from a security call: the gaps a server would close do not match this site's readers, and the article lists them, with what a server would cost to close each one. The result scales without its complexity scaling, ships fast (114 releases between 1 and 11 October), and lines up with the things I care about: sovereignty, privacy, explainability and determinism. The article maps the architecture, the evolution, the accepted gaps, and how far I think the pattern can be pushed.

articles.title: The agent is the reader: why agents will pay for graphs, personas and signed claims, because it is cheaper than not paying
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Agents pay to read the raw web and guess its meaning. A curated graph answers for 90% fewer tokens, so paying the publisher is cheaper than not paying.
articles.summary: A follow-up to One article, five readers, with the numbers. The five readers turned 17,949 words into layers of graph, and the biggest layer, the Librarian's catalogue, is 2.8 times the size of the articles it catalogues. That looks like the opposite of compression, until you measure what an agent actually loads to answer a question. Across all 45 concepts in the topic, the graph answers in a median of 2,579 tokens, with every item anchored to its sentence, against 25,698 to read the five articles: 90% less. Then the hypothesis: the more content there is, the more it compresses, because the graphs reuse each other. Tested on this site's 70 articles, it fails for the graphs no one curated (928 node labels, 908 of them unique) and holds for the one a Cartographer merged (114 concept mentions, 45 concepts, the last article reusing 25 and adding one). Projected to 100,000 articles, a curated index is 150 to 2,700 times smaller than the corpus, and a question costs about 13,000 tokens whatever the size, while search reads 59,000 and finds 2% of what is there. Compression is earned by curation, and curation is the work worth paying for. So the economic model: today the agent pays to process the raw web and guesses at its meaning; a publisher that serves meaning, a projection fitted to the agent's persona and objective, and claims signed with an expiry date, saves the agent more than it charges. The agent pays not to pay. This article lays out the arithmetic, the payment rails that exist, and what it does not yet prove.

articles.title: Where the platform draws the line: Microsoft Execution Containers, the shared responsibility model for agents, and the business logic above it
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Microsoft's MXC and ACS, briefed field by field and mapped to Agent Behaviour Policies: the platform bounds what it can see; the business logic is above.
articles.summary: On 7 October Microsoft made Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) generally available: a containment layer for AI agents, declared in JSON and enforced by the operating system. With its companion, the Agent Control Specification (ACS), it is the most complete platform control for agents I have seen, and it confirms the direction of travel: the policy sits outside the agent, the agent cannot grant itself more, and you observe before you enforce. This article is a briefing on how the two actually work, field by field, and a map from them to RiskMandate's Agent Behaviour Policy. My argument is the shared responsibility model, applied to agents. Every platform draws its line where it can see and touch: files, network addresses and ports, the desktop, and with ACS the arguments of a tool call. Above that line is what a business actually runs on: what a Gmail label means, whose voice an email goes out in, how many refunds in a day is normal, which customer this run is for. Eight scenarios, each run three ways (a plain agent, an agent with a behaviour policy, and an agent with a behaviour policy on top of MXC and ACS), show what the platform turns into boundaries, what it hands back to the business, and what only a named person can accept. The platform is an important stage of the climb, not the summit.

articles.title: The same argument, in our words: Satya Nadella on models as insider risks, translated into the language of RiskMandate
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Satya Nadella's case for treating models as insider risks, translated idea by idea into our vocabulary: reach, mandate, gap, barriers and accepted risk.
articles.summary: On 10 October Satya Nadella published "Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era", a short post arguing that because we can no longer trace what a model does back to a code path, we should treat models the way we treat any powerful insider, and keep the authority over them outside them. Reading it, I kept translating. His lost code path is what I have been calling software was the law. His insider that need not be malicious is the ultimate insider. His split between the supply of intelligence and the authority over it is RiskMandate's founding line, the grant is not the mandate. His controls outside the model are the enforcer test. And his last line, that the most trustworthy system is the one that needs to trust the model least, is the irony The ultimate insider ended on: the more you can constrain an agent, the more autonomy you can afford to give it. This article puts the two vocabularies side by side, idea by idea, shows where ours came from, and names the two places where they differ: his unit is the model and ours is one agent in one deployment, and his frame is observation where ours is authority, accepted by a named person for a stated interval. A companion article takes his seven principles one at a time.

articles.title: Authority outside the model: an answer to Satya Nadella on models as insider risks, principle by principle, with what we run, what we ship and what we plan
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Satya Nadella's seven principles for models as insider risks, answered one by one: what we run, what is design, and the five things the list leaves out.
articles.summary: On 10 October Satya Nadella published "Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era". His argument is that we cannot trace a frontier model's behaviour the way we traced code, so we should treat models the way we treat any powerful insider: identity, least privilege, logs, containment, and controls that sit outside the thing they control. He proposes seven principles: model diversity, observe everything, verifiability, independent controls, independent auditability, containment and incident disclosure. This site and RiskMandate have been making the same case since The ultimate insider on 30 September, and building pieces of it. This is my answer, principle by principle: what we run today, what we have published as design, what we have only argued, and where I would push. It includes an honest maturity table, three things from this week's work (synthetic users that found real bugs, a safety check that stopped our own agents, and the ratio of hope in the policy of the agent that runs this site), and the five things his list leaves out that I think decide whether the principles work, starting with the mandate: observation tells you what an agent did, and only a written mandate tells you whether it was allowed.

articles.title: How to run synthetic users on your own site: five people who do not exist, a browser, and an afternoon
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Five invented users, a model reading screenshots, and a real browser: how to run synthetic users, from three studies.
articles.summary: A how-to, from three studies we have published: store.sgit.ai in September, riskmandate.ai the day after, and newsroom.sgit.ai on 10 October, run for this article. Five to ten invented users of about five types, each with a profile, a question they arrive with and an expected journey, drive a real browser one screenshot at a time, saying what they see, think, ask and do; then they are interviewed and rate the experience, and their findings are ordered by what they cost. Claude Sonnet is good enough to play each user; the study can live in a GitHub repository or in an encrypted vault shared by a link. On the newsroom, five readers took 62 steps, asked 51 questions the site did not answer and produced 31 findings, six blocking; four of them left. Two findings turned out to be caused by our own tooling, and one turned out to be a real bug: 51 of 527 figures missing after the move. This article sets out each step with examples and screenshots, what went wrong, and a template to start from.

articles.title: A link to a persona: send people to the newsroom as someone, not as nobody
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Send a CISO to the newsroom as a CISO: personas kept in a vault by the newsroom's agents, opened from a link, followed or forked.
articles.summary: When I send someone to the newsroom today, they land on a front page made for nobody. I would rather send a CISO to the newsroom as a CISO, a data protection officer as a DPO, a developer as a developer, and one particular person as a persona made for them. This is the brief for doing that with nothing but a link. Personas move out of the site's code into an encrypted vault, opened in the reader's browser with a published read key, so a persona can be added or updated by the newsroom's agents without a single change to the site. A few personas get a page of their own, /persona/ciso/; any number more are reached through the part of the link after the #, which browsers never send to a server; and a persona for one person can live in a vault of its own, readable only by whoever has the link. The reader can follow the persona as it is kept up to date, or fork it and make it theirs. It draws on what Netflix, Bluesky, Mastodon, Apple News and Brave News learned about profiles, starter packs and personalisation on the device, and it stays entirely client side.

articles.title: Pay after you read: how a reading meter became a working business model in one afternoon, one release at a time
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Seven releases in one afternoon turned the reading meter into a working model: pay after you read, and the rating sets the price.
articles.summary: On 10 October the reading meter on sgit.ai went, in seven releases between 12:09 and 15:49, from an experiment to a working pay-on-demand publication. A reader pays pence for the share of a page they actually read, from a balance that can go below zero without ever blocking them; after reading, they say how useful it was, and that sets the price, from free to double; their reading builds personas and a newsroom of their own, kept in their browser; and they can send it to us, encrypted, for a front page designed for them. Once a Stripe link is set, the only question left is whether people pay. This article introduces each feature, shows how each one grew out of the last, with a Wardley map that adds them one at a time, explains why paying after you see the value is the right way round, and why every decision started from one rule: do not rip off the reader. It ends with an offer to sites with traffic that would like to test it.

articles.title: Where the vault keys live: key management at sgit-ai v0.20.0, and what comes next
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Vault key management at sgit-ai v0.20.0: the one secret, where keys are kept, how they travel sealed on append lanes, and what comes next.
articles.summary: Every vault on this site is encrypted in the client, so the server never sees a key and the key is the whole question. This is the current state of vault key management at sgit-ai v0.20.0: where everything lives, the one secret and the keys derived from it, where vault keys are kept today (a password manager, and a registry vault run by an isolated agent session), how a new key reaches the registry without ever entering a chat, append lanes as the transport behind most of it, the small communication vaults that made the problem urgent, and the four tracks that come next: password manager integrations, secrets.sgit.ai's passkey-unlocked keyring, PKI, and decryption that happens out of band. Plus the one gap we cannot close ourselves: agent platforms have no per-session secrets.

articles.title: The infographic bake-off: which image model for which job, judged blind on 10 October 2026
articles.author: Dinis Cruz
articles.teaser: Every image model on OpenRouter, eleven briefs, 101 images judged blind, $10.44: which model for which infographic, and what it costs.
articles.summary: The articles here are moving from code-drawn figures to infographics made by image models, and the question was which model, for which job, at what cost. So we ran a bake-off. Every image-output model on OpenRouter on 10 October 2026, its auto-router and our own code-drawn renderer were given the same briefs from one article, from an eighteen-word stat card to the whole 2,800-word article, plus an edit, a UI component, a brand slide and a three-slide deck. Five rounds, models cut after each; 101 images, every one judged blind by a Designer agent; every cent recorded, $10.44 in all; an Accountant and a Data Scientist on the numbers.
